title: Working with mohair yarn
subtitle: How to handle the halo, manage slipping stitches, and correct mistakes in mohair
excerpt: Mohair's halo obscures stitch structure and makes tinking back almost impossible. Work slowly, count carefully, and plan to live with small corrections rather than ripping out.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book.

glossaryTerms.definition: The cloud of fine fluffy fibres that surrounds a mohair or mohair-blend yarn. It creates a soft blurred effect around each stitch.
Unravelling crochet back to a previous point by pulling out the working yarn. Named after the sound 'rip it, rip it'.

content.text: Mohair yarn produces a distinctive soft halo from the long, fine goat fibre. The
blurs the edges between stitches, makes stitch counting harder, and causes the fibres to mesh together when the fabric is handled.
mohair is difficult to impossible because the halo fibres lock together. Plan to work carefully and accept small imperfections rather than ripping out.

Mohair works best on simple stitches with a large hook. The halo fills the spaces in the stitch, so openwork and lace benefit from the texture, while dense stitches like moss stitch can disappear entirely into the halo. Simple treble or double crochet fabrics let the fibre quality show. Avoid mohair for detailed textured work where stitch definition matters.
Use a size 5.0 mm hook or larger, which opens the stitch loops enough to see clearly even through the halo.
Work in good light. The halo absorbs light on the stitch surface, making the V of each stitch hard to see.
Stretch the top of the last row slightly between the fingers to open the stitch loops before inserting the hook. The halo parts to reveal the loops underneath.
Count stitches at the end of every row without exception. Mistakes in mohair are expensive to fix.

Frogging more than one or two rows of mohair is rarely successful. The fibres tangle around each other and the yarn cannot be reused neatly. When a mistake is found several rows back, the practical choice is usually to leave it or to cut the yarn and rejoin at the mistake point, working forward from there with a new yarn join.

items.symptom: The hook keeps catching the halo fibres rather than entering the stitch
items.cause: The hook tip is sharp and penetrates the mohair cloud rather than sliding past it to the stitch loop below.
items.fix: Use a blunter hook tip, or pre-separate the halo from the stitch loop with a finger before inserting the hook.

items.symptom: The mohair is matting together during working
items.cause: The fabric is being handled extensively between stitches, causing the fibres to felt from friction.
items.fix: Handle the worked fabric less. Keep it folded neatly while working rather than bunched in the lap.

content.text: A mohair-silk blend yarn is easier to handle than pure mohair because the silk core stabilises the strand. If working with mohair for the first time, a mohair-silk laceweight held alongside a plain DK gives the halo effect with a much more workable stitch structure.
